title: MA8-13335
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The claimant, XXXXX XXXXX, a citizen of Haiti, alleged a well-founded fear of persecution in his country of citizenship, for reasons of his political opinion.

Believing that he is a "person in need of protection", he is also claiming refugee protection because of a danger of torture, and a risk to his life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment.
The claimant stated that he was attacked on two occasions. His former boss was not able to protect him, so he decided to leave his country.
He fears being kidnapped, and being killed by the kidnappers, the Chimères or the Zinglindos.
The panel determines that the claimant is not a "Convention refugee" or a "person in need of protection" for the following reasons.

The claimant's identity has been established to the panel's satisfaction. Upon his arrival in Canada, he presented his Haitian passport and other identification documents, which were seized by Citizenship and Immigration Canada (CIC). Copies have been placed on the record.

The claimant was also consistent in his statements. Since his arrival, he has stated that he was attacked because he was transporting products and, consequently, he became a prime target for criminal elements. He reiterated the statements that he made initially to the immigration officers and in his reply to question 31 of his Personal Information Form (PIF).

The claimant then stated that, when he was leaving work, he was attacked by some individuals who, when they were committing the offence, identified him as the spouse of someone who had a business and who refused to pay a ransom. The claimant has been consistent in making this statement.

In his testimony, the claimant often alluded to the political situation in his country. When the panel questioned him, he stated explicitly that the risk that he faces is in no way related to political activities or any opinions that he would have expressed or that might be attributed to him.

He stated that, because he is a Jehovah's Witness, he does not participate in politics. Nor does his wife or any other member of his family, as they are all Jehovah's witnesses, and are not involved in any political activities whatsoever.

He is not claiming refugee protection because of his political opinion, as was stated clearly and explicitly when the question was put to him. He did, however, state that he was attacked for the following reasons, although these events did not have a direct link. The attacks, which he claims to have been the subject of, occurred in different areas. According to him, he was attacked three times along the roads that he takes to deliver the merchandise, and each time he was attacked by a different gang, who beat and humiliated him, and allegedly stole the products that he was transporting.

When asked whether these individuals had any other motives, the claimant explained that his country is in such mayhem that everybody does as they please. According to the claimant, he has every reason to believe that his attackers, believing that it was a truck belonging to a non-governmental organization bringing aid to those in need in the Gonaives, intended to pilfer the goods that he was transporting. According to the claimant, the attack that occurred in 2007 while he was waiting for the bus, happened simply because his attackers wanted to steal some money. And that is what they did by taking his wallet and stealing the bills and coins that it contained.

According to the claimant, when they were committing their crime, they did not identify him as the driver for a non-governmental organization (NGO) but, rather, as a business owner who refused to pay the ransom that they were demanding. When the question was put to him, the claimant identified his persecutors as robbers, kidnappers who, in a situation of general mayhem, attack all sectors of the population indiscriminately. Although the claimant alludes to political opinions in his PIF, he recognized that the persecution that he claimed to be subjected to had nothing to do with political activities or opinions that could have been attributed to him or that he could have been associated with for one reason or another.

In making this testimony, the claimant demonstrated that his fear is linked to the endemic crime that is rampant in his country of citizenship. He does not know his persecutors and would not be able to identify them. He only knows that they are robbers, criminals who, in his own words, used to be referred to as Chimères or Zinglindos.

The panel is of the opinion that the risk faced by the claimant is a random risk that, according to the claimant, is faced indiscriminately and generally by all people living in his country. The panel is of the opinion that the claimant did not discharge his burden of proving that he was personally targeted and that the risk that he claims to be subjected to differs from the risk encountered by other people living in his country.

Consequently, the panel determines that the exception under subparagraph 97(1)(b)(ii) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act applies and that the claimant is not a "person in need of protection".

The panel arrived at this conclusion because the claimant did not demonstrate to the panel's satisfaction that he was exposed to a personalized risk that is different from that to which all Haitians are generally exposed.

The risk alleged by the claimant is a random risk that is faced by all people living in that country. It does not target the claimant personally or particularly. In light of the aforementioned, and considering the claimant's testimony, the panel arrived at the following conclusion.

After analyzing all the evidence, the panel determines that the claimant did not discharge his burden of proving that there is a serious possibility that he might be persecuted under one of the Convention grounds. Nor did he demonstrate, on a balance of probabilities that, compared to other members of the population, should he return to Haiti he would personally and distinctly be subjected to a danger of torture, to a risk to his life, or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment.
For all these reasons, the panel determines that the claimant, XXXXX XXXXX, is not a "Convention refugee" or a "person in need of protection".

Consequently, his claim for refugee protection is rejected.
